newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Ratings agencies confirm stable NZ outlook.
newsitem.headline: Ratings agencies confirm stable NZ outlook.

text.p: Sovereign credit rating agencies on Friday confirmed New Zealand's rating outlook as stable despite Thursday's budget and Friday's monetary policy statement that indicated lower growth and lower government surpluses.

Standard & Poor's managing director for sovereign ratings, David Beers, told NZPA that, based on news reports of the budget, the AA-plus rating would not be reviewed and the outlook was stable. He had not examined the budget document itself.
"There would have to have been a drastic change in the fiscal outlook or the broader economic outlook for us to re-think the position, either upwards or downwards," Beers said.
He said sovereign ratings were based on one- to three-year periods rather than individual events. The current rating predated the election and formation of the coalition government.

"When we upgraded the sovereign (rating) it was based upon a view of how the fiscal trajectory was going to evolve well after the election. We expected there to be wiggles, but the key thing was that there continued to be the likelihood the budget would remain in surplus."
Beers said the upgrade had not altered after the election late last year because "we weren't counting in the fabulous surpluses that the Treasury was then projecting".
"The fact that the surpluses have been scaled back since the government has changed doesn't alter our view that the rating is correctly positioned."
Future upgrades would depend on whether the government stuck to its broad fiscal policies over a number of years.
"It's still early days because this is the first budget of the new coalition government."
Senior vice-president for sovereign ratings at Moody's Investor Service, Yves LeMay, said the AA1 rating outlook was also stable.

Moody's viewed the budget as a maintenance of the general policy track set out in the March budget policy statement, in that it maintained surpluses in the medium term, continued to reduce debt and increased spending in some areas.
Lemay said the reduced surplus was due to the general economic cycle rather than an easing of the government's purse. The latter would be more likely to cause concern.
The government's surpluses were still "significant" compared with other countries, he added.
